summary: KisanRadar turns NASA Earth observations into a simple farm-level climate risk read for smallholder farmers in South Asia. A user selects a location, a crop and a sowing date. The app compares current NASA data (GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, NASA POWER weather since 2001, MODIS and Landsat vegetation and surface temperature, GRACE water storage) with the same time of year in past years, and tracks the crop growth stage so heat, vegetation and yield logic applies only when it is biologically relevant. It returns drought, heat, flood and vegetation-stress scores with a confidence level and stage-aware adaptation advice such as Safe Alternate Wetting and Drying, stress-tolerant rice and heat-resilient wheat. Every number shows its dataset, observation date and status. Historical replays of the 2022 Punjab heatwave, the 2022 Pakistan floods and the 2023 Tamil Nadu cyclone use archived NASA data. KisanRadar answers the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA data into practical farm adaptation decisions.
details:
What it does?

KisanRadar is a web app for smallholder farmers and agriculture extension workers in South Asia. You click a location, choose rice, wheat or maize and a sowing date, and it returns four risk scores (drought, heat, flood, vegetation stress), an overall score, a confidence level and plain-language adaptation advice. Result cards show which NASA sources answered, with dataset IDs, observation dates and status.

How it works?

The backend (Python, FastAPI) pulls data from NASA POWER and Google Earth Engine collections for GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, Landsat 8 and 9, and GRACE and GRACE-FO. Each observation is ranked against the same calendar window in past years (POWER since 2001, SMAP since 2015). Crop growth stage is estimated from growing degree days, so heat limits, vegetation stress and yield scenarios apply only in the relevant stage. A 20 mm rainfall floor prevents light showers from triggering flood alerts. When NASA POWER and IMERG rainfall disagree by more than 30 percent and 10 mm, the app flags it and lowers confidence. A forecast from Open-Meteo (not NASA) is shown for the next 7 days.

Adaptation advice

Stage-aware guidance from published agronomy sources: Safe AWD (15-20 percent irrigation water saving), submergence-tolerant Swarna-Sub1, drought-tolerant Sahbhagi Dhan, heat-tolerant wheat and residue mulching, and harvest guidance at maturity. Yield impact is shown only as a literature-based scenario estimate, with the documented 10-35 percent range for the Punjab 2022 event.

Historical replays

Archived NASA data replays the March 2022 Punjab heatwave, the August 2022 Pakistan floods and the December 2023 Cyclone Michaung rainfall. The repository includes timestamped real snapshots (5 locations, 3 replays, fetched 14 Nov 2026) so the app opens without credentials.check here https://kisanradar.onrender.com/

Why it is creative?

It combines several NASA missions with crop-stage logic, so a field sown four days ago is not flagged for low vegetation and a ripening crop is not told to irrigate. A provenance panel makes every score auditable, and the advice is offered in English, Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Punjabi and Telugu (machine-translated, to be verified with local extension services).

Intended impact

Help farmers and extension officers make earlier adaptation decisions (irrigation, variety choice, drainage, harvest timing) using NASA data that is otherwise hard to use.

Limitations

Data resolution is coarse (about 9 km for SMAP, 10 km for IMERG, 50 km for POWER, about 300 km for GRACE, which also ends in September 2024). Results are decision support, not an official forecast. Yield figures are scenario estimates. The 36-38 C vegetative limits and growth-stage windows are model assumptions. SMAP percentiles use a short record.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Google Earth Engine API, Leaflet, Chart.js, Playwright and pytest (15 passing analytics tests), Docker. MIT licensed.

Use of AI tools

ChatGPT, Claude and a Gemini-based coding agent were used for brainstorming, code generation and debugging, documentation and machine translations. A background research brief was compiled with an AI research tool from cited sources. No AI tool generated or altered any NASA data value. No NASA logos or branding are used.
